<<EasyJet Navigates Brexit Turbulence: A Test of Airspace>>

Section 1
EasyJet, the budget airline, braced itself for turbulence. Despite flying a record 80.2 million passengers last year – nearly 10% more than the previous year and filling planes to the brim – profits plummeted by 17%. The culprit? A hefty £100 million loss attributed to the post-Brexit slump in the pound. Chief Executive Carolyn McCall acknowledged "a difficult year for the aviation industry," yet positioned easyJet as strategically ahead. McCall emphasized their leading position at major European airports, customer focused friendly service and efficient sustainable cost control. Amid industry bankruptcies and operational struggles for some airlines, easyJet aimed to not only survive, but thrive.

Section 2
The financial downturn, revealed in the figures showing profits before tax falling from £494m to £408m, forced EasyJet to **dare** greatly. Even with lower dollar fuel prices, the weakened pound added £101m to costs. A crucial strategic shift would be required post-Brexit: ensuring EasyJet is majority owned and controlled by EU nationals after 2019. This could alter the structure of the entire airline **society**. The situation feels a bit like **fishing** in the dark waters of the post-Brexit landscape, requiring agile moves to survive. Stelios Haji-Ioannou, the founder holding UK-Cypriot nationality, is expected to be classed as EU-owned, covering about a third of shares. The **tower** of legal and financial arrangements needed a complete re-arrangement.

Section 3
EasyJet plans to ask its 2018 AGM for powers to compel UK shareholders to sell if necessary, solidifying its European operational base. McCall downplayed the potential drama, calling it "a technical, administrative thing" and expressed "no concerns" about securing enough EU shareholders. Early trading saw shares jump by more than 5%, fueled by high forward bookings and improved revenue in the current financial year, "primarily as a result of some capacity leaving the market." This news gave a sweet **treat** to investors. Whether EasyJet can truly navigate the Brexit storm remains to be seen, it is clear they are prepared to alter the airline's foundational structure to maintain their position in Europe.
